passage:
Before. Two days before Diwali, the Sharma family group had 214 unread messages. Swati scrolled: sweet recipes, a baby photo, then a forwarded video about the opposition, then three uncles arguing in capital letters. Her cousin Ojas had left the group once already. She put the phone down, tired to her bones.

During. On Diwali morning, a new forward arrived claiming a minister had banned firecrackers nationwide. Swati checked; it was false. She typed carefully: "Happy Diwali, everyone! 🪔 Small request: can we keep this group for family news and photos, and check before forwarding? Love you all." Then she posted a picture of Dadi's rangoli.

After. A week later, the group was calmer. One uncle still sent forwards now and then; Swati replied with a photo of her dinner and moved on. Ojas messaged her privately: "Rejoined. It's nice again." She grinned and muted only the uncle's late-night videos.

qa.q: How many unread messages did the family group have two days before Diwali?
qa.a: 214 unread messages.

qa.q: How did Swati feel as she scrolled the group before Diwali?
qa.a: She felt exhausted and weary, loving her family but worn out by the arguments and forwards.

qa.q: Which of Swati's gentle rules worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking warmly to keep the group for family news and to check before forwarding worked, because it set a limit without shaming anyone.

qa.q: How might Ojas see the change in the group?
qa.a: Ojas seems relieved and glad, rejoining because the group felt "nice again".

grounding: Across three days, the passage shows a young woman who loves her family but is tired of political forwards, setting gentle rules and changing the subject warmly.

passage:
"Anirban, put the phone down for a minute and listen to your old aunt.

When I was twenty-five, we didn't have phone groups. We had Holi lunch at your great-grandfather's house, forty people and one long table. Every year the men argued about elections until someone cried. I loved them all and I dreaded that lunch.

One year I, Vidya, the youngest daughter-in-law, did something new. When your grandfather started on the ruling party, I stood up and said, 'Papa, no politics till the gujiyas are finished. Tell us about your first Holi instead.' Everyone laughed. He told the story. Nobody fought.

I did it every year after that. They called it Vidya's rule.

So when your family group gets noisy, beta, you don't need to win. Change the subject kindly. It works better than you'd think."

qa.q: What did Vidya ask Papa to talk about instead of politics?
qa.a: His first Holi.

qa.q: What did Vidya feel about the Holi lunch before that year?
qa.a: She loved everyone there but dreaded the lunch, because the arguments always ended with someone crying.

qa.q: Which choice at the Holi lunch changed things, and why did it work?
qa.a: Vidya standing up to warmly change the subject worked, because it was light and loving, not a scolding, so everyone laughed and joined in.

qa.q: How might Vidya's father-in-law have seen her interruption?
qa.a: He may have felt honoured to be asked for his story, which is why he told it instead of arguing.

grounding: An elder recalls being tired of family political fights at festivals and setting a warm rule to change the subject, which kept love and peace at the table.

passage:
"People ask how Sabina and I are still friends. I'm Parul, and honestly, I asked myself the same thing last year.

We met in hostel. Ten years of chai, heartbreaks, exams. Then the election came and we realised we vote completely differently. She wants lower taxes and less government. I want more spending on public hospitals. We had one awful evening where we both said things we regretted.

I went home and sat with a question: what do I actually need from a friend? And the answer was, I need her to respect people. Not to agree with me on budgets.

So I called her. We talked about what really mattered to each of us. She said she'd never mock anyone for being poor. I believed her. She's the first person who came when my father was in hospital.

We still argue about tax. Loudly. Then we order dessert."

qa.q: What does Parul want more spending on?
qa.a: Public hospitals.

qa.q: How did Parul feel after the awful evening with Sabina?
qa.a: Parul felt shaken and regretful, unsure whether the friendship could survive their political differences.

qa.q: What helped Parul decide the friendship could continue?
qa.a: Deciding which values truly mattered, respect for people, and talking openly with Sabina about them, rather than needing agreement on policy.

qa.q: How might Sabina see their friendship now?
qa.a: Sabina likely values it deeply, since she was the first to come to the hospital, and enjoys arguing about tax without it threatening their bond 🙂.

grounding: The spoken account shows someone whose close friend has opposing views, deciding which values matter and letting policy differences coexist with care and respect.

passage:
Monday. At Sharmila's birthday dinner, the talk drifted to migrants in the city. Sharmila laughed and said a crude thing about "those people" and how they smelled. Sabina's fork stopped. Everyone else laughed along. Sabina said nothing and went home feeling sick.

Wednesday. She could not sleep. Sharmila had been her closest friend since school. They had disagreed about elections before and it never mattered. This felt different. This was about whether people were treated with dignity.

Friday. She asked Sharmila to walk with her by the lake. "The joke about migrants hurt me. My grandfather came to this city with one bag. I can handle us voting differently. I can't laugh at people like that."

Sharmila went quiet for a long time. "I didn't think. I'm sorry." Then, "Tell me about your grandfather."

They walked until dark.

qa.q: On which day did Sabina ask Sharmila to walk by the lake?
qa.a: On Friday.

qa.q: Why couldn't Sabina sleep on Wednesday?
qa.a: She felt torn and troubled, because Sharmila was her closest friend, but the joke touched on dignity, which mattered more to her than election differences.

qa.q: What did Sabina do that gave the friendship a chance?
qa.a: She raised the issue openly and calmly, explaining that differences in voting were fine but mocking people's dignity was not.

qa.q: How does Sharmila see the moment by the lake?
qa.a: Sharmila seems ashamed of the joke once she hears Sabina's hurt and her grandfather's story, and wants to understand.

grounding: Across several days, the passage shows someone deciding which values truly matter in a friendship with opposing views and speaking openly when the issue is dignity.

passage:
Astrid had a poster of the young mayor on her fridge in Gothenburg. She had knocked on doors for her campaign, cried at the victory party, and still wore the green badge on her backpack.

So when the mayor announced closing three neighbourhood libraries to fund a new stadium, Astrid felt it like a punch.

"You're going to defend it?" Nkechi asked over lunch, eyebrows up.

"No," Astrid said slowly. "I think it's wrong. The library in Hammarkullen is where half the kids do homework."

"But she's your hero."

"She's still the best we've had. And she's wrong about this."

That evening Astrid wrote a letter to the city council, signed with her name and her volunteer number. She kept the badge on her backpack. It felt heavier, and somehow more honest.

qa.q: How many neighbourhood libraries did the mayor plan to close?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: What did Astrid feel when the mayor announced the library closures?
qa.a: She felt shocked and hurt, as if punched, because she admired the mayor and had worked for her campaign.

qa.q: What did Astrid's letter show about healthy support for a leader?
qa.a: It showed that you can keep supporting a leader while criticising a specific decision, which is not betrayal.

qa.q: How does Nkechi see Astrid's position?
qa.a: Nkechi is surprised and a little sceptical, expecting Astrid to defend her hero, and then sees her disagree honestly.

grounding: The passage shows someone who admires a leader and feels part of the cause but keeps the ability to criticise a specific act without seeing it as betrayal.

passage:
The district party office in Madurai was crowded with volunteers folding pamphlets. Lakshmi had been there every evening for a month. The state leader's speech on women's education had made her cry, and she had signed up the next morning.

Tonight the local secretary read out a new order: all volunteers must share the leader's video attacking a journalist by name.

Pooja, folding beside her, whispered, "Isn't that journalist the one who got threats last year?"

Lakshmi felt her stomach drop. She still believed in the schools plan. But this?

She raised her hand. "Sir, I'll share the education videos gladly. I won't share this one. Attacking one journalist by name isn't what drew me here."

The room went quiet. The secretary frowned. "Noted."

Afterwards Pooja squeezed her arm. Lakshmi went home proud and uneasy in equal measure, but she came back the next evening.

qa.q: What were the volunteers told to share?
qa.a: The leader's video attacking a journalist by name.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel when she refused to share the video?
qa.a: She felt proud and uneasy in equal measure, still believing in the schools plan but troubled by the attack on the journalist.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi get right in how she disagreed?
qa.a: She stayed loyal to the parts she believed in, like the education videos, while openly refusing one specific act she thought was wrong.

qa.q: How might Pooja see Lakshmi raising her hand?
qa.a: Pooja likely admired her courage and felt relieved someone said it aloud, which is why she squeezed Lakshmi's arm.

grounding: The passage shows a volunteer who sincerely admires a leader but keeps the ability to criticise a specific act, treating disagreement as loyalty to the cause, not betrayal.

passage:
The rain in Bhopal came down in sheets, and Jyoti had forty doors left on her list before sunset. Her umbrella had broken at door twelve.

At door thirty, an old man with a hearing aid invited her onto the veranda. "Your party says it will fix the drains," he said. "They said that five years ago too."

Jyoti opened her mouth and heard the slogan coming out, the one they had chanted at the morning meeting. She stopped.

"You're right that it was promised before," she said instead. "I honestly don't know if they'll do it this time. I know the local candidate lives two streets away and floods too."

He laughed. "At least you're honest."

Indu, her canvassing partner, was shivering by the gate. "We won't finish the list," she said.

"Then we won't," Jyoti said. "I'd rather talk properly to fifteen people than shout slogans at forty."

They went home soaked, and oddly happy.

qa.q: At which door did Jyoti's umbrella break?
qa.a: At door twelve.

qa.q: What did Jyoti feel when she heard the slogan coming out of her mouth?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and a little embarrassed, sensing the slogan was replacing real thinking.

qa.q: What did Jyoti do well as a volunteer, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She listened to the voter, admitted the past broken promise honestly and knew her limits about the list, which built more trust than slogans.

qa.q: How does the old man see Jyoti's answer?
qa.a: He appreciates her honesty, laughing that at least she didn't just repeat promises.

grounding: Under heavy rain and a long list, the passage shows a volunteer who finds energy in a movement, listens to voters, canvasses honestly and catches slogans replacing thought.

passage:
Ankita had joined the climate collective in Kolkata six months ago, and it had given her a new family. Weekend clean-ups, late-night poster painting, friends who argued about river pollution over puchka.

On Sunday morning she saw the photo: someone from the collective had spray-painted "MURDERERS" across the gate of a small plastics factory in Howrah. The owner's family lived upstairs.

In the group chat, people cheered. "They deserve it."

Ankita felt the pull to add a heart. These were her people. Instead she typed, "I'm with you on plastics. But this was wrong. A family lives there."

Her friend Aadhya called within a minute. "Are you trying to split us?"

"No. I'm trying to stay honest. If the other side did this to us, we'd call it vandalism."

Aadhya was quiet. "Maybe. Let's bring it up at Thursday's meeting."

Ankita hung up, heart racing, but sure.

qa.q: What word was spray-painted on the factory gate?
qa.a: "MURDERERS".

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling when people in the chat cheered?
qa.a: She felt torn, pulled to belong and add a heart, but uneasy because a family lived at the factory.

qa.q: What would you advise Ankita for Thursday's meeting?
qa.a: Keep the tone calm, say she still shares the goal, and ask the group to agree that damaging a family's home is not their method 🤔.

qa.q: How does Aadhya see Ankita's message at first?
qa.a: Aadhya fears it might split the group, then begins to consider that Ankita may be right.

grounding: The passage shows a volunteer who draws energy and friendship from a movement but refuses to excuse her own side's wrongdoing.

passage:
The streetlight outside Omkar's building in Thane had been dead for four months. Every night the aunties walked home in the dark, holding their phones up as torches.

"Why bother complaining?" his flatmate Raghav said. "Nothing changes. They're all useless."

Omkar almost agreed. Then he saw a notice for the ward committee meeting on Saturday.

He went. Twenty people in a hot school hall, a tired councillor, a list of complaints. He waited two hours, read out the address, and showed photos of the dark lane. The clerk wrote it down.

Nothing happened for three weeks. Omkar filed the complaint again online and brought two neighbours to the next meeting.

On a Tuesday night, walking home, he looked up. The light was on.

Raghav came out onto the balcony. "Huh."

"Small," Omkar said. "But it works if you keep showing up."

qa.q: How long had the streetlight been dead?
qa.a: Four months.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling when he saw the light on?
qa.a: He felt quietly proud and satisfied, seeing that his small, repeated effort had worked.

qa.q: What small steps helped fix the streetlight?
qa.a: Going to the ward meeting, showing photos, filing the complaint again, and bringing neighbours to the next meeting.

qa.q: How might Raghav see civic effort after the light came on?
qa.a: Raghav, who thought everyone was useless, may feel surprised and a little less cynical after seeing it work.

grounding: The passage shows someone choosing to attend local meetings and report a problem repeatedly instead of withdrawing cynically, and seeing the small civic act work.

"You're really going to stand in that queue?" Deepika asked, leaning in Mohit's doorway. "It's forty degrees."

"It's the municipal election. The line moves fast before noon."

"They're all crooks. Voting just encourages them."

"Maybe some are. But last night I read all four candidates' papers. One of them actually has a plan for the water tanks in our area."

"And if they don't keep it?"

"Then next time I'll vote for someone else. If I sit home, the people who do vote choose for me."

Deepika rolled her eyes. "You sound like a school poster."

"I know." He laughed. "Come with me. We'll get cold coffee after."

She hesitated. "I don't even know who's standing."

"I'll show you the papers. Ten minutes. Then you decide."

She sat down on the step beside him and held out her hand for the phone.

qa.q: Why did Deepika hesitate before sitting down beside Mohit?

qa.q: Which choice does the passage show as wiser, and why?

qa.q: What would change if Mohit stayed home like Deepika suggested?
qa.a: The people who did vote would choose for him, and the candidate with a plan for the water tanks might lose without his informed vote.

grounding: The dialogue shows a young man participating in a local election with informed choices rather than cynical withdrawal, and gently drawing a friend in.

Samir had filmed the potholes on the road to the Nashik mandi to show the panchayat. He posted it with one angry line about "lazy officials." By morning, forty thousand people had shared it. Half of them now said he was mocking the contractor's caste. Some said worse.

His phone buzzed without stopping. He sat under the neem tree outside the post office, hands cold, reading one message after another.

Francis, the postmaster and his old football coach, came out. "You look like a ghost."

Samir showed him. One message said they would "visit" his family.

Francis took the phone gently and turned off the notifications. "First, we save that message. Then we go to the police station together, now. And you tell your parents today."

"What about replying?"

"Not today. Not scared. Later, if you need to, one calm line."

They walked to the station side by side.

qa.q: Where did Samir sit while reading the messages?
qa.a: Under the neem tree outside the post office.

qa.q: How did Samir feel as the messages kept coming?
qa.a: He felt frightened and isolated, his hands cold, especially when one message threatened to "visit" his family.

qa.q: What did Francis advise Samir to do, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Turn off notifications, save the threat, report it to the police together, tell his parents that day, and not reply in panic, which protected him and brought in help.

qa.q: How does Francis see Samir's situation?
qa.a: Francis sees that Samir is scared and in real danger from the threat, and treats it as something to act on the same day.

grounding: The passage shows a young man whose post goes viral for the wrong reasons, feeling afraid and isolated, and an older mentor helping him step away, save evidence, report threats and not reply in panic.

"Don't read them," Ishita said, reaching for Kunal's phone.

"They found my college tweets," he said. "From when I was nineteen. The stupid joke about the hostel mess. Now they're saying I hate the cooks."

"Did you mean it that way?"

"No! But it doesn't matter. Someone called me garbage. Someone posted my old address."

Ishita sat on the arm of the sofa. "Kunal. They've read three lines of your life. They don't know you drove Amma to dialysis every week for two years."

"I feel like nothing."

"I know. Here's what we'll do. You write one line: the joke was old, badly worded, and you're sorry for how it sounds. One. Then mute everything."

"And then?"

"Then you call Dr. Mehra's counselling line like you did last year. And we watch old cricket matches until you sleep."

He typed the line. She took the phone and turned it face down.

qa.q: How old was Kunal when he wrote the college tweets?
qa.a: Nineteen.

qa.q: What does Kunal's "I feel like nothing" show about how he feels?
qa.a: It shows he feels ashamed and worthless under the strangers' attacks.

qa.q: What was wise about Ishita's plan?
qa.a: She had Kunal correct the facts once, mute the attackers, and reach out to his counselling line, instead of arguing or reading more.

qa.q: How does Ishita see the mob's attack on Kunal?
qa.a: Ishita sees it as based on a fragment of his life, three old lines, not the person who drove Amma to dialysis every week.

grounding: The dialogue shows a young man attacked online over an old post who feels worthless, and his sister helping him correct the facts once, mute and seek support.

passage:
I'm Raghav. Two years ago, for about ten days, I was the most hated person on my city's internet.

I had reviewed a small café honestly, a bit harshly. The owner posted my review with my photo. By evening, people had found my school, my old girlfriend's comments, a blurry photo of me at a party at eighteen. Strangers called me a spoiled rich kid. I'm a bank clerk.

I stopped eating. I read every comment, believing each one.

My friend Anand came over on day three, took my phone, and said, "They're reading one page of a very long book."

That stuck. I posted one short correction: I'm not rich, the review was about the food, I'm sorry it came across so harsh. Then I muted everything and started seeing a counsellor.

By day ten, the storm had moved on to someone else. I hadn't.

qa.q: What was Raghav's job?
qa.a: A bank clerk.

qa.q: How did Raghav feel in the first days of the attack?
qa.a: Raghav felt worthless and ashamed, believing every comment and unable to eat.

qa.q: What steps helped Raghav get through it?
qa.a: Posting one short correction, muting everything, seeing a counsellor, and leaning on Anand's support.

qa.q: What would change if Anand had not come over?
qa.a: Raghav might have kept reading every comment alone, sinking deeper into shame without the reminder that the mob only saw a fragment.

grounding: The reflective account shows someone called names and having their past dug up online, feeling worthless, correcting facts once, muting and seeking support.

passage:
Newsroom note from the social media desk, Thursday

This morning a video went round of a school principal in Pune scolding a student. Within an hour, thousands were calling for the principal's arrest. Elizabeth, our newest trainee, drafted a post for our page: "Shameful! This man should never teach again." She was angry, and it came from a good place.

Before she posted, I asked two questions: do we know what happened before the clip starts, and would we say this to his face? She paused, then rang the school.

The full clip showed the student had just shoved a younger child down the stairs. The scolding was sharp but not cruel.

Elizabeth went red. "I almost joined a mob."

We posted a short factual report instead, with both clips. I told her the instinct to defend a child was right; the rush was the problem. She has asked to write the verification checklist for the team.

Ira, desk editor

qa.q: What did Elizabeth's draft post say?
qa.a: "Shameful! This man should never teach again."

qa.q: What did Elizabeth feel when she learned the full story?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and shaken, going red as she realised she had almost joined a mob.

qa.q: What did Ira's two questions help Elizabeth do?
qa.a: They made her pause and check the full story, so the team posted a proportionate, factual report instead of joining the pile-on.

qa.q: How might the principal have been affected if Elizabeth's post had gone up?
qa.a: The principal could have faced even more hatred and threats for a moment that, in full, was sharp but not cruel.

grounding: The note shows a young trainee who feels righteous anger at a pile-on and nearly joins it, then pauses to check the full story and responds with facts and proportion.

Diary. Pooja. Sunday night, feeling a bit sick with myself.

This afternoon everyone was sharing a video of a woman yelling at a delivery rider outside a café in Bandra. The comments were brutal: her face, her clothes, her company name. I was furious for the rider. I typed "hope she loses her job, disgusting person" and my thumb was over Post.

Then Ayesha sent me a longer version. The rider had knocked her elderly mother over with his bike and was driving off. She was still wrong to scream the things she did. But it wasn't the whole story.

Would I have said "disgusting person" to her face? Never.

I deleted my comment. Instead I wrote one line under Ayesha's post: "Longer clip here. Yelling was wrong, but so is this pile-on."

Three people called me a sellout. I'm okay with that.

qa.q: What did the longer video show?

passage:
Every Friday Yamini posted the Sirsi town news on the local community page: rainfall, market prices, school results, who needed blood donors. Four thousand people followed it.

On Saturday morning, Pallavi-teacher, retired from the girls' school, stopped Yamini outside the vegetable shop. "Your post said the dam gates open Monday. The notice at the taluk office says Wednesday. Farmers downstream might move their cattle too early."

Yamini's cheeks went hot. She had rushed that post at midnight.

"Are you sure?" slipped out, sharper than she meant.

Pallavi-teacher just held out her phone with a photo of the notice.

Yamini looked, then breathed out. "You're right. Thank you, really."

She posted the correction before she even reached home: "Correction: dam gates open WEDNESDAY, not Monday. My mistake. Thanks to a reader for pointing it out." By evening, more people had shared the correction than the original.

qa.q: According to the taluk office notice, when would the dam gates open?
qa.a: On Wednesday.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling when Pallavi-teacher pointed out the error?
qa.a: Yamini felt embarrassed and a bit defensive, her cheeks going hot and "Are you sure?" slipping out sharply.

qa.q: What did Yamini get right after checking the notice?
qa.a: She thanked Pallavi-teacher and posted a clear correction right away, owning the mistake openly.

qa.q: How might Pallavi-teacher see Yamini's quick correction?
qa.a: Pallavi-teacher may feel respected and reassured that the farmers would get the right date, and trust the page more.

grounding: The passage shows someone whose public work contains a genuine error, politely pointed out; it stings, but she thanks the critic, fixes it and publishes a correction.

passage:
Monday. A reporter quoted Pallavi out of context from a panel on hospital staffing, and by noon the clip was trending: "Young nurse says patients are a burden." She sat in the hospital locker room, heart pounding, writing a furious reply on her phone.

Her colleague Harsha found her. "Don't post that. Not today."

Tuesday. Pallavi barely slept. Would they fire her? She booked a meeting with HR and brought the full recording of the panel. The HR officer listened, then said, "We'll handle media questions. Please don't comment publicly for now."

Friday. The hospital released a short factual statement with the full quote: she had said overworked staff struggled to give patients the time they deserve. The clip slowly stopped trending.

Pallavi deleted the angry draft. Harsha brought her a samosa. "Silence and calm," Harsha said. "Hardest thing ever."

qa.q: What did Pallavi bring to the HR meeting?
qa.a: The full recording of the panel.

qa.q: What was Pallavi worried about on Tuesday?
qa.a: She was anxious and frightened that she might be fired and her reputation ruined over the out-of-context clip.

qa.q: Which choices helped Pallavi through the controversy?
qa.a: Not posting the angry reply, speaking with HR, and letting the hospital release a short factual statement with the full quote.

qa.q: How does Harsha see the week?
qa.a: Harsha sees how hard it was for Pallavi to stay silent and calm, and supports her with advice and a samosa.

grounding: Across several days, the passage shows a young nurse afraid for her job after a controversy, speaking with HR, avoiding angry rebuttals and letting a short factual statement speak.

passage:
"Ganga, you're worried about that post at work? Sit down. Let me tell you about 1998.

I, Santosh, was twenty-four, a junior engineer at the municipal corporation. A newspaper printed that I had approved a bridge that later cracked. Half true. I had flagged the cracks in a report; my senior ignored it.

My name was in the paper. People at the tea stall stared. I wanted to write a long angry letter to the editor listing everyone who was really at fault. I wrote four pages that night.

My father read it and said, 'Tear it. Go see the union lawyer tomorrow.'

I did. The lawyer helped me send a short statement with a copy of my report. Three lines. No blame, no anger.

The inquiry cleared me in two months. The four pages? Still in a drawer. I read them when I'm tempted to reply in a hurry."

qa.q: What did Santosh's father say to do with the letter?
qa.a: Tear it, and go see the union lawyer the next day.

qa.q: What did young Santosh feel when his name was in the paper?
qa.a: Santosh felt humiliated and angry, with people staring at the tea stall and a strong urge to blame others in a long letter.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Santosh, and why?
qa.a: Going to the union lawyer and sending a short, factual statement with the report, instead of an angry letter, which helped the inquiry clear Santosh.

qa.q: How might Santosh's father have seen the four-page letter?
qa.a: The father may have been worried it would make things worse and wanted Santosh to answer calmly with proper help.

grounding: An elder recalls fearing for a job and reputation after a controversy, and choosing a lawyer's help and a short factual statement over an angry rebuttal.
